content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases in children. Studies indicate that 64% of infants experience at least one episode of AOM by the age of six months, and this figure rises to 86% by the age of one year. Although bacterial infections are the primary cause of AOM, viral infections often act as the initial trigger. While AOM is typically self-limiting in most children, it carries a risk of complications. The widespread use of antibiotics to treat AOM has raised concerns about increasing antibiotic resistance. Influenza vaccines have been proposed as a potential strategy to reduce the incidence of AOM by preventing the viral infections that often precede it. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of influenza vaccines in reducing the occurrence of AOM in infants and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and ClinicalTrials.gov, as of February 15, 2017. Reference lists of included studies were also reviewed to identify additional trials. The study included randomized controlled trials that compared influenza vaccines with either placebo or no treatment in children under six years of age. Participants included children of any sex, ethnicity, and history of recurrent AOM. Two independent reviewers screened the studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Statistical analyses were performed using both random-effects and fixed-effect models, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB), all with 95% confidence intervals (CI). A total of 11 trials were included, involving 17,123 children aged six months to six years. Six trials were conducted in high-income countries, while five were multicenter trials spanning high-, middle-, and low-income countries. Eight trials recruited participants from healthcare settings. Ten trials, including all four that contributed to the primary outcome, received funding from vaccine manufacturers. Four trials reported adequate allocation concealment, and 10 trials ensured adequate blinding of participants and personnel. Attrition rates were low in eight of the trials included in the analysis. The primary outcome revealed a modest reduction in the occurrence of at least one episode of AOM over a follow-up period of at least six months. This was based on data from four trials involving 3,134 children (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.02; RD -0.04, 95% CI -0.08 to -0.00; NNTB 25, 95% CI 12.5 to 100). The evidence quality for this outcome was judged to be low. Subgroup analyses, including the number of vaccine doses and types of vaccines administered, showed no significant differences. There was a reduction in antibiotic use among vaccinated children, as reported in two trials involving 1,223 children (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.83; RD -0.11, 95% CI -0.16 to -0.06). The evidence quality for this outcome was considered moderate. However, the study was unable to determine whether there was any significant difference in healthcare utilization between vaccinated and unvaccinated children. The use of influenza vaccines was associated with a statistically significant increase in fever (7 trials, 10,615 children; RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.24; RD 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.04) and rhinorrhea (6 trials, 10,563 children; RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.29; RD 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.16). Both outcomes were supported by low-quality evidence. No significant difference was observed in the incidence of pharyngitis. Importantly, no major adverse events were reported. The original review included subgroup analyses of AOM episodes by season and vaccine type, but these were removed in the updated review due to the limited number of trials. Additionally, one study (Belshe 2000) was excluded from the primary and secondary outcomes because it reported AOM episodes per person rather than per group. Adverse events were analyzed individually rather than as a subgroup. In conclusion, influenza vaccination results in a small reduction in the incidence of AOM in children. The observed reduction in antibiotic use is noteworthy, particularly in the context of current guidelines aimed at minimizing antibiotic overuse. However, the safety data from these trials were limited, and the benefits of influenza vaccination for AOM prevention must be weighed against its efficacy in reducing influenza and its safety profile. The quality of evidence was judged to be low to moderate, and further research is needed to clarify these findings.
